title: How to Estimate Taxes on Your 401(k), IRA, and Roth Withdrawals
description: Calculating your 'Blended Tax Rate' in retirement.
content:
Your retirement expenses are paid with 'Net' dollars, but your balances are usually 'Gross' dollars. A $1 Million Traditional 401(k) is not worth $1 Million to you; it is worth $1 Million minus the IRS's share (often 20-30%). Understanding how different accounts are taxed—Ordinary Income vs. Capital Gains vs. Tax-Free—is critical for determining how much you can actually spend. This guide helps you calculate your 'effective' retirement tax rate.

Key Takeaways

  • Ordinary Income (The Expensive Bucket): Traditional 401(k), Traditional IRA, and Pension withdrawals are taxed just like wages (10% - 37%). This is usually your highest tax liability.
  • Capital Gains (The Efficient Bucket): Sales from a Taxable Brokerage account are taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20%. This is often lower than your income tax rate.
  • Tax-Free (The Best Bucket): Roth IRA, Roth 401(k), and HSA withdrawals (for medical) are 0% tax. Social Security is also partially tax-free depending on income.
  • The Standard Deduction: The first ~$29,200 (married) of income is tax-free. Always fill this bucket with Traditional withdrawals first.

Why It Matters (US Context)

State taxes matter. Withdrawals are taxed by your state of residence, not where you worked. Moving from California to Florida before withdrawing your 401(k) saves you ~10% instantly.

The Withdrawal Tax Simulator

Scenario: You need $100,000 to spend. Married Couple.

Source 1: Social Security ($40k)

Taxable portion depends on 'Provisional Income'.
Likely 85% taxable ($34k added to AGI).

Source 2: Traditional IRA ($40k)

100% Taxable as Ordinary Income. ($40k added to AGI).
Total AGI: $74,000.
Taxable Income (after $29k Standard Deduction): $45,000.

Source 3: Roth IRA ($20k)

0% Taxable. Does not add to AGI.

The Bill

Taxable Income: $45,000.
Bracket: 12%.
Tax Due: ~$5,000.
Effective Rate: 5% on $100k spend.

Insight: You lived on $100,000 but only paid $5,000 in tax. This is the power of tax diversification.

Optimization Moves

  1. Fill the Brackets: Withdraw Traditional money up to the top of the 12% bracket ($94k taxable income). If you need more, pull from Roth to avoid jumping to 22%.
  2. 0% Capital Gains: If your taxable income stays under ~$94k, selling stock in your Brokerage account incurs $0 federal tax. This is a huge 'hidden' bracket.
  3. Withholding: Set up automatic withholding on your 401(k) withdrawals (e.g., 15%). It is easier than paying quarterly estimated taxes.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do RMDs force taxes?

Yes. At 73, you MUST withdraw a %, which creates taxable income. This can push you into higher brackets or trigger IRMAA surcharges.

Is Social Security tax-free?

Only if your other income is very low (<$32k combined). For most middle-class retirees, 50-85% of the benefit is taxed.

Can I move states to avoid tax?

Yes. Federal law prevents states from taxing non-resident pension/401k income. If you earned it in NY but live in FL, you pay 0% state tax.
